script: I staged a bombastic revenge, and the bully's reaction stunned everyone.. I got a gig at 18 in the Canadian oil patch, pumping $20 an hour with zero schooling. I was the new kid on the crew, 6'1" and a baby face, paired with Gary—an overweight, lazy, mid‑50s alcoholic who thought he was the boss. He spent most of his shift in the trailer watching DVDs, napping, and typing data. When I'd lift a 250‑lb pipe, he'd just stare and snicker. Gary started calling me stupid because I'd never used a power drill. "Did your dad teach you anything?" he'd say. I told him my dad was only in my life for a few years, and he laughed, "No wonder he left." I didn't have the confidence back then to fight back, so I just kept quiet and did the job. He drove us to work in his truck, paid us a penny a kilometer, and hung over every morning. I'd drive 100–350 km a day, while he slept like a gin‑bloated corpse. After three months of insults and abuse, I reached my breaking point. I told him I'd rather drive home than work with him. He threatened my job, and I was like, "Fine, I'll just get out of here." I wanted to leave, not revenge, but the next morning, when Gary was still in his travel coma, I saw a semi‑truck pulling into a pull‑out a few kilometers from the site. The trucker was outside, the rig was running. I had an idea. I parked Gary's truck right next to the semi, turned on the beacon, and the trucker's headlights flooded the road. Then I blew my horn like a damn war drum, and I screamed, "Fuck! We're going to die!" The sound was louder than a horn on a battlefield. Gary, still half‑asleep, heard it and jolted upright, his face turning white as a sheet. He tried to get out, but the truck was already moving, and the airhorn hit the air in his ears. He screamed, "What the hell is happening?" and I laughed so hard I could barely breathe. He'd been so quiet, so full of threats, that I could just make fun of him. I told him, "You can't even handle a joke." He tried to threaten me again, but I was laughing. He finally got to the site, ordered me out, said I was fired, and stormed off to call the company owner. I sat in the truck, smoking a cigarette, feeling like a king for the next four hours while the owner drove up. The owner was a medium‑sized businessman, the GM of the crew. Gary tried to involve the cops for "attempted murder," but the owner shut him down. Gary's story made me look like a villain, but I knew he'd never be the same. I got moved to a different crew, where I could be the lone sociopath and earn some street cred among the boys. I tricked my bully into thinking he was about to die in a motor vehicle collision with a semi‑truck. I did what I had to do to survive, and that's the tea.
